groups.text: A checkout is a chain: get the FX rate, convert, round to cents, charge.
Each stage runs when the one before it hands it a value.
Now the FX call fails with a five hundred two.
Which of the next three steps run?
None. The failure skips every thenApply: their functions never run, and their futures fail with the same cause.
It slides down to the handlers.
whenComplete only looks, and passes it on.
exceptionally catches it, but this late, all it can return is: declined.
Move exceptionally up, right after the FX call.
Now it returns the last known rate, and every later step runs as if nothing went wrong.
A future is only a box for the answer.
The work runs somewhere else, on an io thread.
With orTimeout of two hundred ms, a timer fills the box with a TimeoutException at two hundred ms, and it travels down the chain like any failure.
The call never hears about it.
It keeps its thread until six hundred ms, and then its answer is thrown away.
A timeout ends the wait, not the work.
So give the client its own timeout too.
Now ask three FX providers at once, and wait for all three with allOf.
flaky fails at fifty ms.
alpha answers at one hundred, beta at three hundred.
allOf waits for all three, then fails, because one failed.
One bad answer at fifty ms fails the whole call, three hundred ms later.
The fix: put a handle on each call first.
It turns a failure into an empty answer, so allOf can only succeed.
Now flaky's failure comes out of its handle as an empty answer, and at three hundred ms the next step picks the lowest price.
Give each call its own orTimeout too, so a provider that hangs becomes one more empty answer.
In Java or Kotlin, each call gets its deadline, then its handle.
The rule. A failure skips every stage until a handler catches it.
Catch it where you still have a useful answer.
Check yourself. The first stage fails, then comes thenApply A, then exceptionally, then thenApply B.
Which of A and B runs?
Only B. A is skipped, and exceptionally hands B a value.
